# nish/net/quic

The server side of a QUIC version 1 connection (RFC 9000, RFC 9001, RFC 9221): the TLS 1.3 handshake carried in CRYPTO frames at three encryption levels, transport parameters both ways, acknowledgements per packet number space, the connection-ID table, streams both ways (`nish/net/quic-stream`) and DATAGRAM frames once the handshake is done. Sans-IO, like the rest of `nish/net`.

<scalar-code-group>

```ts example.ts
import { QuicConnection, QuicServerConfig } from "nish/net/quic";
import { tlsSignEcdsaP256 } from "nish/net/tls";

const conn = new QuicConnection(config, entropy);   // entropy: QUIC_CONN_ENTROPY_SIZE random bytes
conn.receiveWindow(buf, off, len, now);              // every datagram the client sends; now in ms
const input: u8[] | null = conn.signatureInput();
if (input !== null) {
  const signature: u8[] | null = tlsSignEcdsaP256(key, input);   // key: Secret<u8[]>
  if (signature !== null) { conn.sign(signature); }
}
let n: i32 = conn.takeDatagramInto(out, 0, now);     // out: at least QUIC_CONN_DATAGRAM_SIZE bytes
while (n > 0) { … send out[0 .. n) to the client … ; n = conn.takeDatagramInto(out, 0, now); }
let id: i64 = conn.nextStreamEvent();                 // a stream with news: read it, write it
… conn.streamRead(id, buf, 0, size) / conn.streamWrite(id, data, 0, n, fin) …
… and at conn.deadline(), conn.handleTimer(now); once done, conn.reset(entropy) for the next peer
```

<scalar-detail title="What it is">

One connection, from the client's first Initial to a
CONNECTION_CLOSE either way. The handshake is `nish/net/tls`'s `TlsServer`,
driven over QUIC as RFC 9001 §4 describes: the bytes it writes at each
level go out in CRYPTO frames of the matching packet number space, the
bytes the client sends in CRYPTO frames are put back in order and handed to
it, and each level's packet keys are made with `nish/net/quic-packet`'s
`quicKeys` as soon as `TlsServer` knows the secret. The server's transport
parameters, `original_destination_connection_id` and
`initial_source_connection_id` among them, go into EncryptedExtensions; the
client's are parsed and checked (RFC 9000 §7.3, §7.4) before the server's
flight leaves.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Streams">

They are `nish/net/quic-stream`'s: both kinds, opened by either
side, with flow control per stream and for the connection raised as the
application reads, and the stream limits raised as streams finish. The
application sees them through a small surface: `nextStreamEvent` names a
stream with something new (opened, readable, finished, reset, stopped, or
writable again), `streamRead` and `streamWrite` move bytes a chunk at a
time with back-pressure, `openStream` opens one of the server's,
`streamReset` and `streamStopSending` abandon a side. `readStream` and
`writeStream` are the all-at-once forms, which allocate.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Datagrams">

**Datagrams** (RFC 9221). With `maxDatagramFrameSize` above 0 the server
advertises `max_datagram_frame_size` and takes DATAGRAM frames up to it; a
DATAGRAM frame it did not offer to take, or one larger, is
PROTOCOL_VIOLATION. `sendDatagram` queues a payload when the client
offered to take one that size and it fits a packet; it goes out within the
congestion window, and is never sent again. `readDatagram` hands out what
arrived. Each way is a fixed ring (`nish/net/quic-datagram`).

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Loss recovery">

**Loss recovery** (RFC 9002). It is `nish/net/quic-recovery`'s: every
ack-eliciting packet is recorded in its space's ring with what it carried
(its CRYPTO range, its STREAM chunks, HANDSHAKE_DONE and the control frames),
the client's ACKs give the RTT estimate and show what was lost by packet or
time threshold, and what a lost packet carried is sent again, from the CRYPTO
bytes a level keeps until it is discarded and the bytes a stream keeps until
they are acknowledged; a control frame goes again with its current value.

When nothing is acknowledged for a probe timeout, with its backoff,
everything in flight is queued again and a probe goes out in each space that
has packets in flight, a PING if there is nothing to resend (§6.2.4) — two
datagrams of them during the handshake, each with the oldest CRYPTO data not
acknowledged. A client that shows it lacks the server's handshake data (an
Initial repeating CRYPTO data, an ack-eliciting Handshake packet) gets it
again at once, a datagram each time, up to `QUIC_CONN_EARLY_RESENDS` times
(§6.2.3).

NewReno's window holds back everything ack-eliciting but a probe; an ACK
always goes. PATH_RESPONSE and DATAGRAM are never sent again (RFC 9000 §13.3,
RFC 9221 §5.2). Pacing, and GSO batching, are the carrier's:
`nish/net/quic-listener`. Once the 1-RTT keys are in, one Application Data
packet number in every 128 to 1024 is skipped, at a distance drawn from the
ID seed, and the last `QUIC_CONN_SKIP_RING` are remembered: an ACK of one
acknowledges a packet never sent, an optimistic ACK meant to widen the
congestion window, and is PROTOCOL_VIOLATION (RFC 9000 §21.4).

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Nothing allocated per packet">

**Nothing allocated per packet** (QUIC-3). A connection is a slot: every
buffer it uses — the packet record, the CRYPTO reassembly, the connection-ID
table, the datagram rings — is made by the constructor and reused, and
`reset` makes the slot a new connection for the next peer.

The stream buffers are borrowed instead (`QuicStreamPools` in
`nish/net/quic-stream`): a receive side takes one on its first byte and a
send side on its first write, each goes back zeroed once the stream is done
with it, and a server's connections share one set of pools, so idle slots
hold none. A standalone connection makes private pools as large as all its
slots at its first packet. The pools are primed before a packet's arena block
and never touched inside it.

A packet is opened (`receiveWindow`) and a datagram built and sealed
(`takeDatagramInto`) inside a `using a = arena()` block, so the AEAD's and
the header protection's temporaries go when the block ends, and the compiler
refuses the block if anything in it could store one.

The handshake keeps its state in the slot too: one `TlsServer`, made by the
slot's first handshake and `restart`ed by each after it; every level's packet
keys, and a key update's, derived in place into `QuicKeysSlot`s
(`nish/net/quic-packet`) over the slot's HKDF scratch; the Initial secrets,
the stateless reset tokens and the connection IDs computed in arena blocks;
the transport parameters encoded and parsed into the slot's own objects.
After the first connection in a slot, a connection keeps nothing at all
(QUIC-3 in `docs/security/quic.md`).

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Time">

The connection has no clock: `receive`, `takeDatagram` and
`handleTimer` take the caller's monotonic time in milliseconds, and
`deadline()` says when `handleTimer` is next due. Five things run on it. The
idle timeout (RFC 9000 §10.1) is the smaller of the two sides'
`max_idle_timeout`, never under `QUIC_CONN_IDLE_FLOOR` or three probe
timeouts; once it passes with nothing received, the connection closes
silently (`QUIC_STATE_TIMED_OUT`) and wipes its keys. Loss recovery's timer
declares packets lost by the time threshold or fires the probe timeout.

After a key update the previous read keys are kept for a probe timeout
(`recovery.probeTimeout()`), for packets the network reordered, before the
next generation's are derived (RFC 9001 §6.5). And while a new path is
validated, its PATH_CHALLENGE goes again a probe timeout after the last, and
validation gives up max(3 PTO, 6 kInitialRtt) after the move (RFC 9000
§8.2.4, §9.3.2).

Once the connection has closed, by either side, its keys are kept through the
closing or draining period, three probe timeouts (RFC 9000 §10.2), and wiped
at its end; `deadline()` is that end, then -1. A close this side owes starts
the period when `takeDatagram` sends it, not when `close` or `fail` is
called, so that however long the caller waits, the close still goes out.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Key update">

**Key update** (RFC 9001 §6), both ways. A 1-RTT packet whose Key Phase bit
differs from the current one is opened with the next generation's read keys,
which are derived ahead of time so that a forged bit costs no derivation and
shows no timing difference (§6.3); if it opens, the client has updated, and
the server's write keys follow before anything is acknowledged (§6.2).
`updateKeys()` starts an update from the server once the client has
acknowledged a packet of the current phase (§6.1).

The generations take turns in two key slots and two secrets a direction, so
an update keeps nothing in the arena; each still costs two key derivations of
work, so a connection takes at most `QUIC_CONN_MAX_KEY_UPDATES` updates the
client starts and closes on the next with KEY_UPDATE_ERROR (QUIC-4).

The AEAD limits are kept (RFC 9001 §6.6): from three quarters of AES-GCM's
confidentiality limit, 2^23 packets under one write key, the server starts an
update itself, and closes with AEAD_LIMIT_REACHED, sealing nothing more, if
it reaches the limit with none possible; past the integrity limit of packets
that fail to authenticate over the connection, 2^52 for AES-GCM and 2^36 for
ChaCha20-Poly1305, it closes with AEAD_LIMIT_REACHED too.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Sans-IO and deterministic">

No socket, no clock and no random device:
every random choice (the TLS server random and ephemeral key, the server's
first connection ID, and the seed later IDs are derived from) comes from
the `entropy` the constructor and `reset` take, every stateless reset
token from the configuration's static key (RFC 9000 §10.3.2), and every
ACK says a delay of zero. So a recorded exchange replays byte for byte.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Paths">

**Paths** (RFC 9000 §8.2, §9). `receiveWindowFrom` takes the 18-byte
`nish:net` address each datagram came from, and `sendAddress()` says where
the connection's datagrams go: the first Initial's address, validated by the
handshake, until the client's address changes. Before the handshake is
confirmed a datagram from any other address is dropped unread, so no forged
source moves a handshake or takes its flight.

After it, a datagram from a new address whose newest non-probing packet
authenticates moves the connection there (§9.3) — a later one from the old
address, with a lower packet number, does not move it back — and a
PATH_CHALLENGE, eight bytes from the ID seed's HMAC, padded to 1,200 bytes,
validates the new path.

Until a PATH_RESPONSE with any of the last three challenges' data arrives, on
any path, the server sends there at most three times what came from it
(§9.3.1); a lost challenge is drawn again, fresh, a probe timeout later; past
max(3 PTO, 6 kInitialRtt) validation has failed and the connection goes back
to the last validated address, where the client — or, for a forged source,
the real client's next packet — finds it.

Validated, a new address starts congestion control and the RTT estimate
again, a port-only change keeps them (§9.4), and ECN is tested again
(§13.4.2). A packet that carries only probing frames moves nothing: its
PATH_CHALLENGE is answered on its own path, alone in a datagram
`takeProbeInto` writes for `probeAddress`, under that path's own 3x limit.
The client's connection ID is kept across a move (§9.5): a NAT rebinding
gives the client no reason to change it, and this server never migrates
itself. Every address, challenge and counter is a field made by the
constructor and cleared by `reset`.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="What a peer cannot do">

Nothing it sends makes this module panic. A
datagram that does not parse, a packet that does not authenticate, a
duplicate packet number, a packet for keys already discarded and a 1-RTT
packet before the handshake is done are dropped and counted in `dropped`. A
frame that breaks the protocol closes the connection with the transport error
RFC 9000 names (`QUIC_ERROR_*` in `nish/net/quic-frame`), a TLS alert closes
it with CRYPTO_ERROR (0x100 + the alert), and the CONNECTION_CLOSE is the
next datagram out.

Before the client's address is validated — by a Handshake packet, or by a
Retry token `nish/net/quic-listener` checked — the server sends at most three
times what it received (§8.1). Every buffer a peer can fill is fixed: CRYPTO
reassembly by `QUIC_CONN_CRYPTO_WINDOW`, each stream by the credit advertised
(its buffer), the connection by `maxData`, the connection-ID table by the
limit advertised, the received packet numbers by `QUIC_ACK_MAX_RANGES`, and
datagrams by their ring.

</scalar-detail>

<scalar-detail title="Secrets">

The packet keys of each level live in this connection's key
slots as long as the level does; so do the 1-RTT secrets the next key
generation is derived from, and the next generation's read keys. The traffic
secrets and the ephemeral key `TlsServer` holds are `Secret` fields its
`wipe()` reaches (TLS-1): `afterTls` takes each level's secrets out of them
once, into this connection's plain slots, and zeroes them through
`wipeSecret`.

The slots are plain bytes, wiped with stores no optimiser removes
(`secureZero`, and `aesKeyWipe` for an AES schedule): each level's key, IV,
header-protection key and schedules when the level is discarded; each
generation's key, IV, schedule and secret when a key update replaces it; and
the rest — the 1-RTT keys, the key-update secrets, whatever `TlsServer` still
holds and the connection-ID seed — by `release()`, `reset`, the idle timeout,
and the end of the closing or draining period (RFC 9000 §10.2), three probe
timeouts after this side's CONNECTION_CLOSE went out or the client's arrived.
`docs/security/quic.md` records what is wiped where as QUIC-2.

</scalar-detail>

Written from RFC 9000, RFC 9001 and RFC 9221, in this module's own
structure; nothing here is ported from another implementation. Private
names carry the `quicConn` prefix (`docs/wp26-stdlib.md` §3e).

## Functions

### quicConnResetTokenInto

`quicStatelessResetToken` of the ID `cid[at .. at + length)` into
`out[outAt ..]`, computed in a connection's own HMAC scratch inside an
arena block, so issuing an ID keeps nothing (QUIC-3). The scratch and the
full MAC are wiped before it returns.

```ts
function quicConnResetTokenInto(
  mac: HmacSha256Scratch,
  key: u8[],
  cid: u8[],
  at: i32,
  length: i32,
  out: u8[],
  outAt: i32,
): void
```

<scalar-field name="mac" type="HmacSha256Scratch" required>

The connection's HMAC-SHA256 scratch, wiped on return.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="key" type="u8[]" required>

The server's static reset key, `QUIC_CONN_STATIC_KEY_SIZE` bytes.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="cid" type="u8[]" required>

The array holding the connection ID.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="at" type="i32" required>

Where the ID starts in `cid`.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="length" type="i32" required>

The ID's length in bytes, at most 20: the caller's to keep, as nothing checks it.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="out" type="u8[]" required>

Where the 16-byte token goes; bytes that would fall past its end are not written.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="outAt" type="i32" required>

Where in `out` the token starts.

</scalar-field>

### quicStatelessResetToken

The stateless reset token for the connection ID `cid` (RFC 9000 §10.3.2):
the first 16 bytes of HMAC-SHA256 under the server's static `key`. A
connection hands it to the client with each ID it issues, and
`nish/net/quic-listener` derives the same token from a packet's ID alone
once the connection is gone, which is what lets a server that lost its
state end the connection.

```ts
function quicStatelessResetToken(
  key: u8[],
  cid: u8[],
): u8[]
```

<scalar-field name="key" type="u8[]" required>

The server's static reset key, `QUIC_CONN_STATIC_KEY_SIZE` bytes
  (`QuicServerConfig.statelessResetKey`).

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="cid" type="u8[]" required>

The connection ID the token is for, all of its bytes.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="u8[]">

A fresh 16-byte token (`QUIC_RESET_TOKEN_SIZE`); the full MAC it was cut from is wiped.

</scalar-field>

## Classes

### QuicConnection

One server connection, which is also a reusable slot. Make one, hand it
every datagram the client sends with `receiveWindow` (or `receive`), sign
when `signatureInput()` asks, send what `takeDatagramInto()` writes until
it answers 0, and use streams and datagrams once `state` is
`QUIC_STATE_CONNECTED`. Once it has closed, `reset` makes it a new
connection for the next client, with its buffers kept.

The fields are readable: `state`, `error` (the transport error or
application code the connection closed with), `dropped`, `alpn` and
`serverName` once the handshake has read them, `peerParameters`, `streams`
(the stream table), and `cids`, the connection-ID table, which a server
that runs many connections routes datagrams by (`ownsConnectionId`).

```ts
class QuicConnection
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new QuicConnection(config: QuicServerConfig, entropy: u8[])` | A connection under `config`, with `entropy` its `QUIC_CONN_ENTROPY_SIZE` random bytes, which are copied out and then wiped in the caller's array. Every buffer the connection will use is made here, sized by `config`. Entropy of another length, or limits outside what `QuicServerConfig` documents, leave the connection closing with INTERNAL_ERROR before it reads anything; it then sends nothing. |
| `addressValidated: boolean` | Whether the client's address is validated: a Handshake packet from it was processed. |
| `alpn: string` | The ALPN protocol the handshake chose. |
| `application: QuicConnSpace` | The Application Data packet number space, which holds the 1-RTT keys. |
| `appReadSlot: i32` | Which of the Application Data space's two read slots, and two write slots, hold the current keys. |
| `appWriteSlot: i32` | Which of the Application Data space's two write slots holds the current keys, 0 or 1. |
| `authFailures: i64` | Packets that failed to authenticate over the connection, against `integrityLimit`. |
| `bytesReceived: i64` | Bytes received and sent, for the anti-amplification limit (RFC 9000 §8.1). |
| `bytesSent: i64` | Bytes sent, which may not pass three times `bytesReceived` before the address is validated. |
| `challengeResendAt: i64` | When the PATH_CHALLENGE goes again with fresh data, and when validation gives up (§8.2.4); -1 when not validating. |
| `challengesDrawn: i64` | How many PATH_CHALLENGE data have been drawn over the connection; see `challengeData`. |
| `challengeUntil: i64` | When path validation gives up, in milliseconds, or -1 when not validating. |
| `cids: QuicCidTable` | The connection IDs of both sides and their stateless reset tokens (`nish/net/quic-conn-cid`). |
| `cidSeed: u8[]` | The 32-byte HMAC key, taken from the entropy, that each new local connection ID is derived from; `release` wipes it. |
| `confidentialityLimit: i64` | The AEAD limits this connection keeps (RFC 9001 §6.6): packets one 1-RTT write key seals, and packets that fail to authenticate over the connection. `afterTls` sets them from the suite when the 1-RTT keys arrive; until then they are AES-GCM's. They are fields so that a test can lower them after the handshake; nothing else should set them. |
| `datagramEcn: i32` | ECN (RFC 9000 §13.4): `ecnMarking` is the carrier's to set when it sends this connection's datagrams with the ECN bits of `datagramEcn`, which each `takeDatagramInto` sets for the datagram it wrote: ECT(0) while loss recovery's `ecnCodepoint()` asks for it, 0 otherwise and always while `ecnMarking` is false. Every packet of a marked datagram is counted as marked, and an ACK_ECN's counts are validated against them. `reset` keeps `ecnMarking`, which is the carrier's, and clears the rest. |
| `datagramsIn: QuicDatagramQueue` | DATAGRAM payloads the client sent, waiting to be read; its `dropped` counts those that found it full. |
| `datagramsOut: QuicDatagramQueue` | DATAGRAM payloads waiting to be sent, and those the client sent waiting to be read. |
| `dropped: i32` | Packets dropped without closing the connection: unparseable, unauthenticated, duplicated, or for keys not held. |
| `earlyResends: i32` | Handshake data sent again early, against `QUIC_CONN_EARLY_RESENDS` (RFC 9002 §6.2.3). |
| `ecnMarking: boolean` | Whether the carrier sends with the ECN bits of `datagramEcn`; the carrier sets it, and `reset` keeps it. |
| `readonly ephemeral: Secret<u8[]>` | The x25519 private key `begin` takes from the entropy, until the handshake hands it to `TlsServer`. |
| `error: i64` | The error code the connection closed with: a transport error, `0x100 + alert`, or the application's code. |
| `errorIsApplication: boolean` | Whether `error` is an application code (CONNECTION_CLOSE 0x1d) rather than a transport error. |
| `handshake: QuicConnSpace` | The Handshake packet number space. |
| `handshakeComplete: boolean` | Whether the handshake is complete, which for a server is also confirmed (RFC 9001 §4.1.2). |
| `initial: QuicConnSpace` | The Initial packet number space: its keys, packet numbers and acknowledgements (RFC 9000 §12.3). |
| `initialClient: u8[]` | The Initial secrets of RFC 9001 §5.2, the client's and the server's. |
| `initialServer: u8[]` | The server's Initial secret (RFC 9001 §5.2); see `initialClient`. |
| `integrityLimit: i64` | Packets that may fail to authenticate before the connection closes (RFC 9001 §6.6). `afterTls` sets it from the suite; a test may lower it after the handshake. |
| `keyUpdates: i32` | Key updates the client started, against `QUIC_CONN_MAX_KEY_UPDATES`. |
| `localEncoded: u8[]` | `localParameters` encoded for the TLS extension the server sends. |
| `localParameters: QuicTransportParameters` | The server's transport parameters, set for each connection, and their encoding. |
| `readonly nextReadSecret256: Secret<u8[]>` | The next generation's 1-RTT read secret under SHA-256, 32 bytes; see `readSecret256`. |
| `readonly nextReadSecret384: Secret<u8[]>` | The next generation's 1-RTT read secret under SHA-384, 48 bytes; see `readSecret256`. |
| `nextSkip: i64` | The next Application Data packet number skipped (RFC 9000 §21.4), or -1 before the 1-RTT keys; a test may set it to force one. `skipped` holds the last `QUIC_CONN_SKIP_RING` skipped, -1 where none, `skipHead` where the next goes, and `skipsDrawn` how many distances were drawn. |
| `now: i64` | The latest time the caller gave, in milliseconds; time never runs backwards here. |
| `otherIsNext: boolean` | Whether `otherReadKeys` are the next generation's rather than the previous one's. |
| `otherReadKeys: QuicKeys \| null` | The other read keys of the Application Data space (RFC 9001 §6.3): the next generation's while `otherIsNext`, and for a probe timeout after an update the previous one's, for reordered packets (§6.5). |
| `pathCount: i32` | How many PATH_CHALLENGE payloads wait to be answered, 0 to 4. |
| `pathKnown: boolean` | Whether `pathCurrent` holds the client's address: the carrier passes addresses, and a first Initial gave one. |
| `pathMtu: i32` | The largest datagram validated on the current path: 1200 until a probe is acknowledged. |
| `pathMtuLimit: i32` | Path MTU discovery (RFC 9000 §14.3, RFC 8899): once the handshake is confirmed and the path validated, the server probes for a datagram larger than 1200 bytes with a PING padded to the size being tried, sent only when nothing else is due, so a probe never holds data back. An acknowledged probe validates its size as `pathMtu`, which every later datagram may then fill; three lost probes of a size end the search below it. A lost probe is no congestion signal (§14.4). Three loss events that each lose a packet larger than 1200 bytes, with none of that size acknowledged between, are taken for a black hole: `pathMtu` falls back to 1200 and the search resumes below the size that stopped getting through. A new address starts again from 1200.<br><br>`pathMtuLimit` is the carrier's to lower, for an interface whose MTU carries less than `QUIC_CONN_DATAGRAM_MAX`: before the first datagram by setting it, and at any time through `setPathMtuLimit`, which also takes a `pathMtu` above it down to it. The next probe keeps under it, and an acknowledged probe raises `pathMtu` no higher than it. 1200 or less turns discovery off. `reset` keeps it. |
| `pathReceived: i64` | Bytes received from and sent to the path being validated, for its own 3x limit (§9.3, §8.1). |
| `pathSent: i64` | Bytes sent to the path being validated, at most three times `pathReceived`. |
| `pathValidated: u8[]` | The last address the client proved it receives at, in `nish:net`'s 18-byte form (RFC 9000 §9): the handshake's, or one a PATH_RESPONSE answered. |
| `pathValidating: boolean` | Whether `pathCurrent` is not validated yet: a PATH_CHALLENGE is out on it. |
| `peerParameters: QuicTransportParameters` | The client's transport parameters, once the handshake has checked them; until then, every default. |
| `pmtuBlackHoles: i32` | Times a black hole sent `pathMtu` back to 1200. |
| `pmtuProbes: i32` | Path MTU probes sent. |
| `pmtuProbesLost: i32` | Path MTU probes declared lost. |
| `probeAddress: u8[]` | A PATH_CHALLENGE that came from another address in a datagram that moved nothing (§9.1): answered there by `takeProbeInto`, from `probeData`, within `probeBudget` bytes, three times what came from `probeAddress` (§8.1). Only the latest such challenge is kept. A response owed on `pathCurrent` when the connection moves goes back the same way (`sendResponsesBack`). |
| `probeOwed: boolean` | Whether a PATH_RESPONSE is owed on `probeAddress`, and whether the datagram being read carried a challenge for it. |
| `readPhase: boolean` | The Key Phase bit of the current read keys, and of the current write keys. |
| `readonly readSecret256: Secret<u8[]>` | The 1-RTT traffic secrets (RFC 9001 §6.1), one set of SHA-256's length and one of SHA-384's, the one the suite's hash picks in use: the current read secret, the next generation's, and the current write secret, which a key update ratchets in place. The write side keeps no next secret, because the server derives its next write keys only when it moves to them. |
| `readonly readSecret384: Secret<u8[]>` | The current 1-RTT read secret under SHA-384, 48 bytes; see `readSecret256`. |
| `recovery: QuicRecovery` | Loss detection, the RTT estimate, the congestion window and the pacer (RFC 9002). |
| `sealedUnderKey: i64` | Packets sealed under the current 1-RTT write key, and packets that failed to authenticate, against those limits. |
| `serverName: string` | The client's `server_name` the handshake read, or empty when it sent none. |
| `skipHead: i32` | Where the next skipped packet number goes in `skipped`. |
| `skipsDrawn: i64` | How many skip distances have been drawn; see `nextSkip`. |
| `state: i32` | Where the connection is in its life: one of the `QUIC_STATE_*` constants. |
| `streams: QuicStreams` | The streams, both ways (`nish/net/quic-stream`). |
| `tls: TlsServer \| null` | The `TlsServer` running this connection's handshake: null until the client's first Initial has opened, and again after `reset`. |
| `tlsSlot: TlsServer \| null` | The slot's `TlsServer`, made by its first handshake and `restart`ed by every one after (QUIC-3). |
| `writePhase: boolean` | The Key Phase bit of the current write keys. |
| `readonly writeSecret256: Secret<u8[]>` | The current 1-RTT write secret under SHA-256, 32 bytes; see `readSecret256`. |
| `readonly writeSecret384: Secret<u8[]>` | The current 1-RTT write secret under SHA-384, 48 bytes; see `readSecret256`. |
| `acceptRetry(originalDcid: u8[], retryScid: u8[]): boolean` | Sets up a connection whose client came back with a Retry token that `nish/net/quic-listener` checked (RFC 9000 §8.1.2): `originalDcid` is the DCID of the client's Initial before the Retry, and `retryScid` the Retry's SCID, which the client now sends to. The server's transport parameters then name both (§7.3), and the client's address counts as validated, so the anti-amplification limit does not apply. Call it before the first `receive`; answers whether it took: not once the connection has started, and not for an ID over 20 bytes. |
| `afterTls(): void` | Whatever TLS's last step made due: its output moved into each level's CRYPTO stream, the keys of each level it now has secrets for, the client's transport parameters checked once it has read them, and, when the handshake completes, the Handshake keys discarded (RFC 9001 §4.9.2), HANDSHAKE_DONE queued (§4.1.2) and the client given more connection IDs. |
| `amplificationBlocked(): boolean` | Whether the anti-amplification limit stops the server sending (RFC 9000 §8.1): the client's address is not validated and three times what it sent leaves no room for a whole datagram. |
| `close(code: i64): void` | Closes the connection from the application, with its own error `code` (CONNECTION_CLOSE 0x1d; RFC 9000 §10.2). The next `takeDatagram` answers the close, and nothing after it. Closing twice, or after the client closed, does nothing. |
| `closed(): boolean` | Whether the connection has closed, either way. |
| `datagramSize(): i32` | The largest datagram the server sends now: `pathMtu`, or 1200 while a new path is being validated. |
| `deadline(): i64` | When `handleTimer` is next due, in the caller's milliseconds: the idle timeout, loss recovery's timer (a time-threshold loss or the probe timeout), the end of a key update's probe timeout, or, while a path is validated, its PATH_CHALLENGE's resend or the end of its validation, whichever comes first; once the connection has closed, the end of its closing or draining period, when its keys are wiped. -1 when nothing is timed: before the first packet, while a closed connection's own close has not gone out (`takeDatagram` sends it), once a closed connection's keys are wiped, and with no idle timeout, nothing in flight, no update pending and no path being validated. |
| `handleTimer(now: i64): void` | Runs whatever is due by `now`, the caller's monotonic time in milliseconds; call it at `deadline()`, or any time. Past the idle timeout the connection closes silently (`QUIC_STATE_TIMED_OUT`, RFC 9000 §10.1): no CONNECTION_CLOSE, every key wiped. Past the closing or draining period of a connection that closed, every key is wiped (§10.2). Past a key update's probe timeout the previous read keys are wiped and the next generation's derived (RFC 9001 §6.5).<br><br>Past loss recovery's timer, packets lost by the time threshold have their frames queued again, or a probe timeout queues every space's packets in flight and asks for a probe (RFC 9002 §6.1.2, §6.2.4): `takeDatagram` then sends it. `receive` and `takeDatagram` run it themselves. Time never runs backwards here: an earlier `now` than one already given counts as that one. |
| `idleDeadline(): i64` | When the idle timeout passes, or -1 when there is none or the timer has not started. |
| `maxDatagramPayload(): i32` | The largest DATAGRAM payload `sendDatagram` takes now: what fits the client's `max_datagram_frame_size` with the frame's type and Length, and a 1-RTT packet of `datagramSize()` with the longest packet number; 0 when the client takes none, or the server sends none. It grows when path MTU discovery validates a larger datagram, and shrinks again on a fall back to 1200, which drops a queued payload that no longer fits. |
| `nextStreamEvent(): i64` | The ID of the next stream with something new for the application — the client opened it, it has bytes or its FIN to read, it was reset or stopped, or it has room to write again after a short write — or -1 when there is none. Each stream comes up once however much happened; read and write it until it has nothing more to say. |
| `openStream(bidirectional: boolean): i64` | Opens a stream of the server's (RFC 9000 §2.1): bidirectional when `bidirectional`, else unidirectional. Answers its ID, or `QUIC_STREAM_ERR_STATE` when not connected, or `QUIC_STREAM_ERR_LIMIT` when the client's MAX_STREAMS is reached (STREAMS_BLOCKED then goes out) or `localStreams` of the server's are open. |
| `ownsConnectionId(dcid: u8[]): boolean` | Whether a datagram whose first packet is sent to `dcid` belongs to this connection: one of its active connection IDs, or, until the handshake is done, the DCID of the client's first Initial. A closed connection still answers for its IDs; the caller drops it once it is done with it. |
| `ownsConnectionIdAt(buf: u8[], at: i32, length: i32): boolean` | `ownsConnectionId` of the ID `buf[at .. at + length)`, read in place, so a carrier routes without a copy. |
| `readDatagram(buf: u8[], at: i32, cap: i32): i32` | Copies the oldest DATAGRAM payload the client sent into `buf` at `at`, at most `cap` bytes, and forgets it. Answers its length, `QUIC_DATAGRAM_NONE` when none is waiting, or `QUIC_DATAGRAM_ERR_ROOM`, keeping it, when it does not fit. |
| `readStream(): QuicStreamData \| null` | The next run of stream data the client sent, or `null` when there is none: the all-at-once form of `nextStreamEvent` and `streamRead`, which allocates the run it answers. `fin` marks the last of its stream; a stream the client reset is passed over. |
| `receive(datagram: u8[], now: i64): i64` | `receiveWindow` of a whole datagram. |
| `receiveWindow(buf: u8[], off: i32, len: i32, now: i64): i64` | Takes one datagram from the client, `buf[off .. off + len)`, which arrived at `now` (the caller's monotonic time in milliseconds): every packet in it is opened and its frames acted on, in order. `buf` is read, never written, so a GRO receive buffer is handed over a datagram at a time. Answers 0, or the error the connection closed with — in which case `takeDatagramInto` writes the CONNECTION_CLOSE to send. A packet that cannot be used is dropped and counted (see the module header). Once the connection has closed, or its idle timeout has passed by `now`, every datagram is ignored. |
| `receiveWindowFrom(buf: u8[], off: i32, len: i32, address: u8[], now: i64): i64` | `receiveWindow` of a datagram that came from `address`, an 18-byte `nish:net` address: the connection follows the client from one address to another (RFC 9000 §9) — see "Paths" in the module header. An address of any other length is no address, as `receiveWindow` gives. |
| `release(): void` | Wipes everything secret the connection and its `TlsServer` still hold: every level's packet keys, the next generation's read keys, the traffic secrets and expected client Finished, the ephemeral key, the connection-ID seed and the stateless reset tokens (QUIC-2). Call it when the connection is done with (or `reset` the slot, which does the same first); the connection is closed after it and sends nothing more. Every stream buffer it borrowed goes back to its pool, zeroed: nothing is sent again from a closed connection. |
| `reset(entropy: u8[]): void` | Makes this slot a new connection for the next client, with `entropy` its `QUIC_CONN_ENTROPY_SIZE` fresh random bytes (wiped in the caller's array): every secret of the last connection is wiped first, as `release()` does, and every buffer is kept and emptied. The limits are the constructor's configuration's. A slot reset this way allocates nothing, and neither does the next handshake (QUIC-3 in `docs/security/quic.md`). |
| `sendAddress(): u8[]` | Where this connection's datagrams go now: the 18-byte `nish:net` address `receiveWindowFrom` last moved it to, or the first Initial's. A carrier sends every datagram of `takeDatagramInto` here; it is empty (all zero) for a connection fed by `receiveWindow` alone. |
| `sendDatagram(buf: u8[], from: i32, length: i32): i32` | Queues `buf[from .. from + length)` as a DATAGRAM (RFC 9221) for the next packet the congestion window allows; it is never sent again if lost. Answers `QUIC_DATAGRAM_OK`, `QUIC_DATAGRAM_ERR_DISABLED` when not connected, the client takes none, or the server takes none and so sends none, `QUIC_DATAGRAM_ERR_TOO_BIG` for a frame past the client's limit or a payload past `maxDatagramPayload()`, or `QUIC_DATAGRAM_ERR_FULL` while the ring holds `QUIC_CONN_DATAGRAM_QUEUE` waiting. |
| `setPathMtuLimit(limit: i32): void` | Sets `pathMtuLimit`, for a carrier whose interface MTU changed. A `pathMtu` above the new limit falls to it, no lower than 1200, and recovery's datagram size with it; the search goes on below it. |
| `sign(signature: u8[]): i64` | Hands the signature over `signatureInput()` to TLS, which writes the rest of the server's flight. Answers 0, or the CRYPTO_ERROR the connection closed with when TLS refused it (a call at the wrong time, or an empty signature: `internal_error`). |
| `signatureInput(): u8[] \| null` | What CertificateVerify must sign while the handshake waits for it, else `null` (see `TlsServer.signatureInput`). |
| `streamRead(id: i64, buf: u8[], at: i32, length: i32): i32` | Reads up to `length` bytes of stream `id` into `buf` from `at`. Answers how many it read, 0 when nothing more has arrived yet, `QUIC_STREAM_END` once every byte up to the FIN was read, `QUIC_STREAM_ERR_RESET` once the client reset the stream (its code is the stream's `resetCode`), or another `QUIC_STREAM_ERR_*`. Reading is what gives the client more credit. |
| `streamReset(id: i64, code: i64): i32` | Abandons stream `id`'s sending side with application error `code` (RESET_STREAM). Answers `QUIC_STREAM_OK` or a `QUIC_STREAM_ERR_*`. |
| `streamStopSending(id: i64, code: i64): i32` | Asks the client to stop sending on stream `id`, with application error `code` (STOP_SENDING). Answers `QUIC_STREAM_OK` or a `QUIC_STREAM_ERR_*`. |
| `streamWrite(id: i64, buf: u8[], from: i32, length: i32, fin: boolean): i32` | Writes up to `length` bytes of `buf` from `from` to stream `id`, and finishes its sending side when `fin` and every byte fit. Answers how many bytes it took — fewer than `length` when the stream's buffer is full, in which case `nextStreamEvent` names it again once acknowledgements free room — or a `QUIC_STREAM_ERR_*`: not connected, an unknown stream, one only the client sends on, one already finished or reset, or one the client asked to stop (STOP_SENDING, which this side answered with RESET_STREAM). |
| `takeDatagram(now: i64): u8[] \| null` | The next datagram to send, or `null` when nothing is due: the allocating form of `takeDatagramInto`, which a test or a recording uses. It is held to `QUIC_CONN_DATAGRAM_SIZE` bytes, so it never sends a path MTU probe nor fills a larger validated path. |
| `takeDatagramInto(out: u8[], at: i32, now: i64): i32` | Writes the next datagram to send into `out` at `at`, which needs `QUIC_CONN_DATAGRAM_SIZE` bytes of room and may take up to `datagramSize()`, or a path MTU probe's size (see `takeDatagramWithin`), and answers its length, or 0 when nothing is due (or the room is not there). Call it until it answers 0 after every `receive`, `sign`, write and `close`. It coalesces an Initial, a Handshake and a 1-RTT packet as each has something to carry, pads a datagram with an ack-eliciting Initial to 1200 bytes (RFC 9000 §14.1), and before the client's address is validated sends only while three times what was received allows (§8.1).<br><br>After a close it writes the CONNECTION_CLOSE once, then nothing. While the handshake waits for a signature it writes nothing, so the server's flight leaves whole. Lost data goes before new data. While the congestion window is full (RFC 9002 §7), or a space's record of packets in flight is, a space sends only an ACK, unless a probe timeout asked it for a probe.<br><br>`now` is the caller's time in milliseconds: a datagram that elicits an acknowledgement restarts the idle timer when it is the first since the client's last packet (RFC 9000 §10.1), and once the idle timeout has passed nothing goes out. The datagram is built and sealed in place, inside an arena block: nothing it does allocates past the call. This is not paced: a carrier that paces calls `nish/net/quic-listener`'s `quicListenerTakeFlight` instead.<br><br>Its contract changed with path MTU discovery: it writes up to the room in `out` from `at`, capped at `datagramSize()` (never past `pathMtuLimit` or `QUIC_CONN_DATAGRAM_MAX`), where it once wrote at most 1200 bytes. A carrier that sizes its buffer from `QUIC_CONN_DATAGRAM_SIZE` keeps getting datagrams of at most that size and is never probed past it; one that hands over a larger buffer must send all of what comes back. |
| `takeDatagramWithin(out: u8[], at: i32, room: i32, now: i64): i32` | `takeDatagramInto` with the datagram held to `room` bytes: it is at most `room` and `datagramSize()`, whichever is less. When nothing else is due and `room` has space for it, the datagram is a path MTU probe (see `pathMtu`), so a carrier that wants probing gives at least `QUIC_CONN_DATAGRAM_MAX` bytes of room, and one that gives 1200 never probes. A probe never displaces data: a sender that always has something due does not probe until it runs out, and stays at 1200 bytes until then. |
| `takeProbeInto(out: u8[], at: i32, now: i64): i32` | Writes the PATH_RESPONSE owed on another path (§8.2.2, §9.1) into `out` at `at`, which needs `QUIC_CONN_DATAGRAM_SIZE` bytes of room, and answers its length, or 0 when none is owed: a 1-RTT packet with that frame alone, padded to 1200 bytes or to three times what came from the path (§8.1), whichever is less. The carrier sends it to `probeAddress`, before `takeDatagramInto`'s datagrams. It is answered once and never sent again (§13.3). |
| `updateKeys(): boolean` | Starts a key update from the server (RFC 9001 §6.1): the write keys move to the next generation and the Key Phase bit of every packet after toggles; the client follows when it reads one. Answers whether it did. It does not while it may not: before the handshake is confirmed, while an update is still in flight (the client has not answered the last one, or answered it less than a probe timeout ago, so the next read keys are not ready), and until the client has acknowledged a packet sent with the current keys. |
| `writeStream(id: i64, data: u8[], fin: boolean): i32` | Queues all of `data` on stream `id`, finishing its sending side when `fin`: the all-or-nothing form of `streamWrite`. Answers `QUIC_STREAM_OK`, or `QUIC_STREAM_ERR_*`: the connection is not connected, the stream is unknown, its side is already finished (or the client stopped it), or the data would pass the credit the client gave for the stream or the connection, or the room in the stream's buffer. |

### QuicStreamData

One run of stream data the client sent, in order, as `readStream` answers it: `fin` when it ends the stream.

```ts
class QuicStreamData
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new QuicStreamData(streamId: i64, data: u8[], fin: boolean)` | A run as `readStream` hands it out. |
| `data: u8[]` | The bytes of the run, in stream order. |
| `fin: boolean` | Whether the run ends the stream: the client sends no bytes after it. |
| `streamId: i64` | The RFC 9000 stream ID the bytes arrived on. |

## Interfaces

### QuicServerConfig

What a QUIC server is configured with, the same for every connection. The
limits are the transport parameters it advertises (RFC 9000 §18.2); the
stream limits and `maxStreamData` also size each connection's buffers,
which are made once and reused.

```ts
interface QuicServerConfig
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `activeConnectionIdLimit: i64` | `active_connection_id_limit`: how many of its connection IDs the client may give the server, 2 to 8. |
| `alpn: string[]` | The ALPN protocols the server speaks, most preferred first; QUIC requires one to match (RFC 9001 §8.1). |
| `certificateChain: u8[][]` | DER certificates, leaf first, as `TlsServerConfig` takes them. |
| `localStreams: i64` | How many streams of its own the server may have open at once, 0 to 1024 (`openStream`). |
| `maxData: i64` | `initial_max_data`: the connection's receive window, 0 to 2^62 − 1, raised as the application reads. |
| `maxDatagramFrameSize: i64` | RFC 9221's `max_datagram_frame_size`: the largest DATAGRAM frame the server takes, 0 (none, and the parameter is not sent) to 1500. The server sends DATAGRAM frames only when it takes them too. |
| `maxIdleTimeout: i64` | `max_idle_timeout` in milliseconds: 0 for none, at most 2^62 − 1. The connection times out after the smaller of this and the client's, and never sooner than `QUIC_CONN_IDLE_FLOOR`. |
| `maxStreamData: i64` | `initial_max_stream_data_bidi_remote` (and `_uni`, and `_bidi_local` when the server opens streams): each stream's receive window and the size of its buffer each way, 1 to 1 MiB. |
| `maxStreamsBidi: i64` | `initial_max_streams_bidi`: how many bidirectional streams the client may have open at once, 0 to 1024. |
| `maxStreamsUni: i64` | `initial_max_streams_uni`: how many unidirectional streams the client may have open at once, 0 to 1024. |
| `retry: boolean` | Whether `nish/net/quic-listener` answers a client's first Initial with a Retry (§8.1.2). |
| `retryTokenKey: u8[]` | The key `nish/net/quic-listener` authenticates its Retry tokens with (§8.1.4), `QUIC_CONN_STATIC_KEY_SIZE` bytes. |
| `retryTokenLifetime: i64` | How long, in milliseconds, a Retry token is accepted after it was issued: 1 to 60000. |
| `signatureScheme: i32` | The signature scheme the caller's key signs with, as `TlsServerConfig` takes it. |
| `statelessResetKey: u8[]` | The static key every stateless reset token is derived from (`quicStatelessResetToken`, RFC 9000 §10.3.2), `QUIC_CONN_STATIC_KEY_SIZE` bytes. Keep it across restarts: a server that lost a connection resets it with the token this key gives for the connection ID the client sends to. |

## Limits

<scalar-grid cols="2">

<scalar-card title="1,452" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_DATAGRAM_MAX: i32`

The largest datagram path MTU discovery searches for: 1452 bytes, what a
1500-byte Ethernet MTU carries under an IPv6 and a UDP header. The search
also stops at `pathMtuLimit` and at the client's `max_udp_payload_size`.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="8" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_DATAGRAM_QUEUE: i32`

How many DATAGRAM payloads each way a connection holds, when it takes any.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="3,000" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_IDLE_FLOOR: i64`

The shortest idle timeout the server keeps: three times the probe timeout
of a path with no RTT sample yet (RFC 9002 §6.2.2, about a second), and
never under three times the current one either. RFC 9000 §10.1 has an
endpoint raise a smaller negotiated value to this, so that several probes
can be lost before the connection is given up.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="4" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_LOCAL_CIDS: i32`

The most connection IDs the server keeps active for the client to use, its own first one included.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="1,500" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_MAX_DATAGRAM_FRAME: i64`

The largest `maxDatagramFrameSize` a configuration may advertise: 1500
bytes, an Ethernet path's whole UDP payload, past which no DATAGRAM frame
reaches a server on a real path. Each of the receive ring's entries is
sized to what is advertised, so every frame taken is held.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="1,024" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_MAX_STREAMS: i64`

The most streams of one kind a configuration may let the client open at once, or open itself.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="67,108,864" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_MAX_STREAM_BUFFERS: i64`

The most bytes of stream buffer a configuration may let each connection
hold: every stream slot (`maxStreamsBidi + maxStreamsUni + localStreams`)
may borrow `maxStreamData` bytes each way, and the pools are sized so all
of them can at once, so a configuration past 64 MiB of them is refused
rather than allowed to allocate it.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="1,048,576" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_MAX_STREAM_DATA: i64`

The largest per-stream credit a configuration may advertise, which is also each stream's buffer each way.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="4" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_PACKET_CONTROL: i32`

The most control frames one packet carries — NEW_CONNECTION_ID,
RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID and the flow-control, limit and stream-ending frames
of `nish/net/quic-stream` — for the same reason: the three new IDs the
server announces once the handshake is done fit one packet, and the rest
go over the next few.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="4" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_PACKET_STREAMS: i32`

The most STREAM frames one packet carries, which is how many chunks a
packet's record keeps for retransmission; the rest of the streams go in
the next packet.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="128" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_SKIP_MIN: i64`

The fewest Application Data packets between two skipped packet numbers
(RFC 9000 §21.4). Large enough that the gaps cost the client almost
nothing in ACK ranges.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="897" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_SKIP_SPREAD: i64`

How many distances past `QUIC_CONN_SKIP_MIN` a skip may fall at: the next
skipped number is `QUIC_CONN_SKIP_MIN` plus 0 to 896 past the number after
the last skip, so skips fall 129 to 1025 numbers apart.

</scalar-card>

</scalar-grid>

## Constants

<scalar-grid cols="2">

<scalar-card title="18" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_ADDRESS_SIZE: i32`

A `nish:net` address: sixteen bytes of IPv6 (IPv4 mapped), then the port, big-endian.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="8" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_CID_LENGTH: i32`

The length of every connection ID this server issues; a short header's DCID is read at this length.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="8,388,608" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_CONFIDENTIALITY_LIMIT: i64`

AES-GCM's confidentiality limit (RFC 9001 §6.6): how many packets one
1-RTT write key seals. The server starts a key update at three quarters of
it, and closes the connection with AEAD_LIMIT_REACHED, sending nothing more
under the key, if it reaches it with no update possible. ChaCha20-Poly1305
has no such limit.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="16,384" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_CRYPTO_WINDOW: i32`

How far ahead of what it has handed TLS the server buffers CRYPTO data.
RFC 9000 §7.5 asks for at least 4096 bytes; a frame past this is
CRYPTO_BUFFER_EXCEEDED. One buffer of this size serves every level, since
the client's Initial flight is complete before its Handshake one starts.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="1,200" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_DATAGRAM_SIZE: i32`

The datagram size every QUIC path carries, and the smallest a client's
first Initial may arrive in (RFC 9000 §14.1): 1200 bytes. The server sends
no larger datagram until path MTU discovery has validated one (`pathMtu`),
and falls back to it when a validated path stops carrying larger ones.
`takeDatagramInto` needs this much room.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="2" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_EARLY_RESENDS: i32`

How many times a connection resends its handshake data before the probe
timeout because the client showed it lacks it (RFC 9002 §6.2.3, "for a
limited number of times per connection"): a client Initial carrying
CRYPTO data the server already read, or an ack-eliciting Handshake packet,
while the server's own CRYPTO data at that level is in flight. Each
resend is one datagram, so a client cannot make the server answer more
than this many packets that way, whatever it sends.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="104" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_ENTROPY_SIZE: i32`

How many random bytes the constructor and `reset` take: 32 for the TLS
server random, 32 for the x25519 key, 8 for the first connection ID and
32 for the seed the later IDs and their reset tokens are derived from.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="2" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_HANDSHAKE_PROBES: i32`

How many ack-eliciting datagrams a probe timeout sends in the Initial and
Handshake spaces (RFC 9002 §6.2.4 allows up to two). The server's first
flight is usually one datagram, so with one probe a lossy path loses every
copy of it about as often as it loses one datagram per probe timeout; two
square that, and stay inside the amplification limit, which a one-datagram
flight and two probes fill exactly. The Application Data space sends one.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="68,719,476,736" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_INTEGRITY_LIMIT_CHACHA: i64`

ChaCha20-Poly1305's integrity limit (RFC 9001 §6.6), 2^36 packets that fail
to authenticate over a connection, across every key, before it closes with
AEAD_LIMIT_REACHED. The connection counts failures against the limit of the AEAD it negotiated.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="4,503,599,627,370,496" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_INTEGRITY_LIMIT_GCM: i64`

The integrity limits (RFC 9001 §6.6): how many packets may fail to
authenticate over a connection's life, across every key, before it closes
with AEAD_LIMIT_REACHED. AES-GCM's is 2^52, ChaCha20-Poly1305's 2^36.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="64" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_MAX_ISSUED_CIDS: i64`

How many connection IDs a connection issues in all, its first included.
The client retiring one asks for a replacement (§5.1.1, a SHOULD), and
each costs two HMACs whose temporaries stay in the arena, so this bounds
what a client can make the server derive by retiring IDs over and over;
past it, a retired ID is not replaced.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="64" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_MAX_KEY_UPDATES: i32`

How many key updates a connection takes from its client (RFC 9001 §6).
Each costs two key derivations of work, though none of their memory, so
the cap bounds what a client can make the server derive (QUIC-4); the next one
closes the connection with KEY_UPDATE_ERROR. A client also has to wait
a probe timeout between two of them.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="8" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_SKIP_RING: i32`

How many skipped packet numbers the server remembers (RFC 9000 §21.4): an
ACK of any of the last this many closes the connection as an optimistic
acknowledgement. One is skipped every `QUIC_CONN_SKIP_MIN` to
`QUIC_CONN_SKIP_MIN + QUIC_CONN_SKIP_SPREAD - 1` packets, so the ring
reaches back at least 7 × 129 = 903 packets.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="32" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_CONN_STATIC_KEY_SIZE: i32`

The length of the configuration's static keys: the stateless reset key and the Retry token key.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="-3" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_DATAGRAM_ERR_DISABLED: i32`

`sendDatagram`: the client did not offer to take DATAGRAM frames (RFC 9221 §3), or the connection is not connected.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="-5" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_DATAGRAM_ERR_FULL: i32`

`sendDatagram`: the send ring is full; try again once a datagram has gone.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="-2" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_DATAGRAM_ERR_ROOM: i32`

`readDatagram`: the next datagram does not fit in the room given; it is kept.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="-4" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_DATAGRAM_ERR_TOO_BIG: i32`

`sendDatagram`: the payload is larger than the client takes, or than fits one packet (`maxDatagramPayload`).

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="-1" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_DATAGRAM_NONE: i32`

`readDatagram`: nothing has arrived.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="0" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_DATAGRAM_OK: i32`

`sendDatagram` queued the payload.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="3" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_STATE_CLOSING: i32`

This side closed the connection: one CONNECTION_CLOSE goes out, then nothing. `error` says why.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="2" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_STATE_CONNECTED: i32`

The handshake is complete and confirmed; stream data flows.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="4" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_STATE_DRAINING: i32`

The client closed the connection: nothing more goes out (RFC 9000 §10.2.2). `error` is its code.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="1" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_STATE_HANDSHAKE: i32`

The handshake is under way.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="5" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_STATE_TIMED_OUT: i32`

The idle timeout passed (RFC 9000 §10.1): the connection closed silently,
its keys wiped, and nothing more goes out. Its state is to be discarded:
drop the connection (or `reset` the slot), so that a later packet to its
IDs reaches `nish/net/quic-listener`, whose stateless reset tells the client.

</scalar-card>

<scalar-card title="0" icon="phosphor/regular/hash">

`QUIC_STATE_WAIT_INITIAL: i32`

Waiting for the client's first Initial packet.

</scalar-card>

</scalar-grid>
